originalGroup.material:
A. Book advice and a bus trip

Asking for a book recommendation can help you discover something outside your usual reading. However, a helpful conversation needs more than the question, "What is a good book?" A few details can give the other person a much better starting point.

Mention a book you recently enjoyed and explain why. The title alone may not reveal what mattered to you. ____1____ Someone who liked the mystery may need a different suggestion from someone who loved the descriptions of a city.

Describe how much time you want to spend reading. You may want a long story for a holiday or short pieces for a daily journey. ____2____ A recommendation is more useful when it fits the situation in which you will actually read.

Ask what makes the suggested book worth trying. Do not feel you must accept it simply because the person sounds enthusiastic. ____3____ That question can reveal whether you are both interested in the same features.

Read a short sample before making a final choice. A summary tells you what happens, but not necessarily how the sentences feel. ____4____ You do not have to finish the whole book to discover whether its style invites you to continue.

Finally, tell the person what you thought after trying it. ____5____ A recommendation can be the beginning of a conversation that becomes more useful as you learn about one another's reading.

B. Book advice and a bus trip

Last Wednesday, my uncle and I ____1____ (take) a bus to the town museum. After ____2____ (wait) for a few minutes, we saw it turn into our street. The bus ____3____ (drive) by a woman who greeted each passenger as they entered.

I had checked the route on my phone, but my uncle carried an old paper timetable. He explained that it could still be useful when a phone had no power. I was not convinced until I noticed how little charge remained in mine.

At the museum stop, we met a volunteer ____4____ coat carried the museum's blue badge. She showed us a map and explained the quickest route through the building. It was such ____5____ interesting introduction that we stayed to ask several questions.

The exhibition included old tickets and photographs of local buses. Some children were looking ____6____ (careful) at a model of a double-decker. Their teacher asked them to compare it with the bus they had used that morning.

Before leaving, we decided ____7____ (buy) a small guidebook. It was ____8____ (cheap) than the large picture book, and easier to carry. My uncle put it beside his timetable. On the journey home, I thanked him ____9____ bringing me. The visit had shown ____10____ (we) something familiar from a different point of view.

originalGroup.material:
A. A small trial and a model boat

Before organising a large activity, you may want to try a small version. A trial can reveal difficulties while changes are still manageable. It is most useful when you decide in advance what you hope to learn, rather than simply asking whether everything went well.

Choose a specific question. If you are planning a workshop, you might want to know whether the instructions are clear or whether there are enough materials. ____1____ The details you record should help answer that question.

Invite people whose experience is relevant to the activity. A task may seem obvious to friends who helped design it. ____2____ Someone encountering it for the first time may notice a missing explanation that the designers no longer see.

Observe before stepping in. It is tempting to rescue a participant as soon as they hesitate. ____3____ Their next action may show you whether they are thinking, searching for an item or misunderstanding a step.

Afterwards, distinguish what you observed from what you think caused it. A person may stop working for several reasons. ____4____ Ask a short question rather than immediately deciding that the instructions were at fault.

Make a small number of changes and keep a note of them. ____5____ Without that record, a later improvement may be welcome but difficult to connect to any particular decision. The point of a trial is not to guarantee a flawless event; it is to make the next plan better informed.

B. A small trial and a model boat

When our class built model boats, we expected the painting to be the ____1____ (enjoyable) part of the project. None of the other stages sounded as much fun. However, testing the first boat gave us a different problem to solve.

We placed it in a shallow tray ____2____ had been filled with water. The boat leaned to one side because we had attached a heavy decoration to its roof. Our teacher suggested ____3____ (remove) the decoration before making any other change.

We followed her advice and tested it again. The second trial was ____4____ (successful) than the first, but we still needed to check whether the boat could carry a small load. Each group was given several ____5____ (coin) to place inside.

Instead ____6____ dropping them all in at once, we added them one by one. A classmate recorded the result after each addition. The model was tested ____7____ (careful), and we kept our hands away from it while it floated.

By the end of the lesson, we ____8____ (discover) that decoration and function had to be considered together. We wrote a short report ____9____ (explain) what we had changed. The teacher asked us to keep both the first drawing and the final notes, so the next class could learn from successes as well ____10____ mistakes.

A. Reading diagrams and a choir score

A diagram can make a complicated idea easier to understand, but it is still a constructed explanation. Before using it as evidence, take a moment to discover how it represents its subject. A few deliberate questions can prevent a quick impression from becoming a mistaken conclusion.

Begin with the title and key. Colours, lines and symbols may have meanings that are not obvious from their appearance. ____1____ A thick line could indicate a main route, a greater quantity or simply a designer's way of separating sections.

Check what the diagram includes. A simplified picture may omit details in order to make one relationship clear. ____2____ Ask whether the missing details matter to the question you are trying to answer.

Notice the difference between position on the page and position in the world. In some diagrams, nearby objects are drawn far apart to keep labels readable. ____3____ The layout may be designed for clarity rather than as a scale map.

Look for information about time when the subject can change. A diagram of a transport network may show routes planned for a future year alongside those already operating. ____4____ Otherwise, a proposal may quietly become a present fact in your reading.

Finally, compare the diagram's claim with another available account. ____5____ A disagreement may reveal an error, a different date or simply a different purpose. Understanding that difference is more useful than deciding that one attractive picture must contain the whole answer.

B. Reading diagrams and a choir score

Having ____1____ (complete) the first rehearsal, our choir gathered around an old handwritten score. Some notes were clear, but a few markings were difficult to read. The conductor, ____2____ grandfather had copied the music many years earlier, explained that we should not simply guess.

What impressed me most ____3____ (be) how patiently she compared the score with another copy. A familiar tune could make an incorrect note sound reasonable, so memory alone was not enough. We learned to distinguish what we expected ____4____ what the page actually showed.

One passage had been marked for a smaller group of singers. At first, that seemed like a chance to do ____5____ (little) work. In practice, hearing fewer voices made each person's entry more noticeable. We had to listen ____6____ (careful) to one another.

The conductor encouraged us ____7____ (practise) the passage in pairs before trying it with the whole group. We worked by ____8____ (we) for a few minutes, then returned to compare what we had noticed.

By the final rehearsal, the uncertain markings ____9____ (check) against the second copy. The performance still required concentration, but the notes no longer concealed an avoidable doubt. I left with a better understanding of ____10____ preparation could support the freedom to sing with confidence.
